extracted.intended_audience: college/university students writing academic papers (undergraduate and graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for achieving clear, effective academic prose by focusing on clarity of meaning, appropriate tone, concision, verb strength, and revision strategies. Covers concrete techniques for locating and correcting common style problems (wordiness, passive voice, nominalization, ostentatious vocabulary, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Say what you mean (clarity of purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your goal in academic writing is not to sound intelligent, but to get your intelligent point across.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imitating complicated, 'smart-sounding' prose that sacrifices comprehension. Focus on communicating and being understood; if you know what you mean but can't yet say it, use writing to discover your point before revising for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a tone suited to the assignment and audience; conversational/chatty language may be inappropriate in many academic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, aim for clear, broadly accessible language. Avoid slang and colloquialisms unless the instructor explicitly invites them. Don't assume a discipline that seems 'artsy' permits creative or casual phrasing; ensure tone doesn't distract from your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordiness (eliminate filler words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using more words than necessary—filler words and phrases that delay the reader from the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate filler words by reading sentences and removing unnecessary small words; write to yourself first to clarify ideas, then rewrite for the reader. Note that wordiness can be a symptom of uncertainty about topic or undeveloped argument; if so, clarify content before trimming. The handout suggests isolating this issue in revision and offers tactics (see clichés, qualifiers, redundant pairs, prepositional phrases, stock phrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichés stand in for more precise descriptions and weaken prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow down and write exactly what you mean; ask 'why?' or 'how?' to replace a cliché with a precise description. Example: replace 'bit off more than it could chew' with 'As the French faltered in Vietnam...'. Read old papers to locate habitual clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overuse of qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive use of qualifiers (very, often, hopefully, practically, basically, really, mostly, etc.) dilutes statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate unnecessary qualifiers to make points stronger and more direct. Some qualifiers are necessary; use them carefully and thoughtfully. Example: 'Most people usually think that many puppies are generally pretty cute.' → 'Most people think that puppies are cute.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant pairs / tautological word pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Using two words that mean the same thing (e.g., 'whole entire') is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the most precise term and delete the extra one. Example: 'Adrienne fulfilled all our hopes and dreams' → 'Adrienne fulfilled all our hopes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Overuse of prepositional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many prepositional phrases in a sentence obscures subject and action and makes the reader work to find the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate by circling prepositional phrases; if several appear in one sentence, rephrase. Ask 'Who did what to whom?' and rewrite to place actor and action nearer each other. Example revision provided in handout (long Gilligan sentence → 'Gilligan hurt the economic system of the island because he couldn’t find adequate resources without angering the headhunters.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock/wordy phrases to replace with single words
rubrics_metrics.description: Many multi-word stock phrases can be replaced by a single more precise word (e.g., 'the reason for' → 'because').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout lists many common replacements (e.g., 'In light of the fact that' → 'because'; 'Prior to' → 'before'; 'It is crucial that' → 'must'). Search your paper for these stock phrases and substitute succinct alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects and verbs visibility (verb trouble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should be able to clearly locate the main subject and verb of sentences; subjects and verbs should ideally be close together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the actor and action are hiding, the reader will struggle. Find subject-verb-object in sentences; if unclear, reorder to make the actor perform the verb. Use active constructions and strong verbs as a baseline until you have control of subtler effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive voice (use strategically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive constructions hide the actor by putting it after the action and often use a 'to be' verb; this can make sentences harder to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate passive voice by circling 'to be' verbs (am, is, are, was, were, be, been, being) and checking if they sit next to another verb (especially ending in -ed). Correct by moving the actor to the subject and removing the 'to be' construction; sometimes passive is acceptable—use it deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominalization (turning actions into nouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive nominalization (making verbs/adjectives into nouns) makes prose abstract and hides action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate by circling nouns; if many nouns in a sentence hide the action, recast the sentence so the action is a verb. Watch for sentence-starters like 'there is/there are/this is/it is' which can indicate nominalization and try to recast (e.g., 'There is a need for further study of aliens.' → 'We need to study aliens further.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak verbs (replace 'to be' and 'have')
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak verbs such as 'to be' and 'have' carry little specific meaning and can make sentences vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate weak verbs by circling 'to be' and 'have' verbs; replace them with more meaningful, specific verbs that state what the subject does. Ask 'What does the subject really do?' Example: 'The aliens have a positive effect on our ecosystem.' → 'The aliens improve our ecosystem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious erudition (do not use words you can’t define)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using multi-syllabic or fancy words without knowing their meanings can make you sound unclear or pretentious and may suggest plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use words you can define and that fit your tone. Don't rely blindly on a thesaurus; repetition of key terms is often preferable to awkward synonyms. Example caution: don't replace 'memory' repeatedly with awkward phrasings just to vary vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize style’s subjectivity and disciplinary variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is partly subjective—different readers, instructors, and disciplines have different expectations (e.g., passive voice used differently in sciences vs. humanities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to instructor and departmental norms; if feedback highlights 'word choice' or 'awk', try to identify specific patterns. Adapt style to the conventions of your discipline and to the specific assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis-before-editing (write to discover then edit for reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordiness and other style problems may stem from uncertainty about topic or underdeveloped argument—use writing to find your point before editing for style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time drafting to clarify what you mean; then rewrite with the reader in mind. If struggling to meet length requirements or clarity, consult assignment-reading strategies or ask instructors/tutors for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focused revision strategy (isolate one style problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: When revising, focus on one recurring style problem at a time (ignore other issues temporarily) to make correction manageable and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit a finished draft for only the selected issue (spelling, punctuation, content aside) using the handout's 'locate and correct' suggestions. As you improve, you will include fewer style problems in initial drafts and need less overall editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reading aloud and tutoring resources to find style problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading your sentences aloud often helps you locate awkward or problematic sentences; tutors can help identify chronic problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try reading your draft aloud before submission. Bring old papers to a writing center appointment so a tutor can show where chronic style problems occur, why, and how to fix them. See the handout on proofreading techniques for more tips.
